Definition / when to use: SHGTF Level 1. Code POLICY DOCUMENTS (HAP, DoE circulars, MoE/NDMA guidance, IMD products, school-held instructions) using the 7-element actionability template. Code only what the text says explicitly; put researcher inference in a memo.
The hazard condition that activates the provision (e.g. heatwave declared, Orange/Red alert, temperature threshold).
Who the provision names as responsible (Education Dept, DoE, DDE, HoS, teacher, SMC...). Note when no school-level actor is named.
What is required or recommended (timing change, suspend outdoor activity, water, ORS...).
Who may authorise the action. Code absence of a stated authority as well.
Resources the provision takes for granted (water, power, fans, ORS, staff, transport).
What happens if the action cannot be done, or for special groups (primary pupils, exams, delayed guardians).
Reporting lines, feedback, after-season review obligations.
RQ1. Readiness established BEFORE any live alert (Sakurai sensei feedback: 'what happens before the disaster?'). Use for both documents and interviews.
Any instruction received before the first in-season alert. Note date and channel.
Named staff responsible for heat; whether an alternate exists.
Written or unwritten school plan for heat.
Pre-season checks or repairs of water points, fans, ventilation, shade, coolers.
Updating phone lists, WhatsApp groups, guardian authorisation before summer.
ORS stock, first-aid kit, link to dispensary/PHC, heat-illness recognition training.
Staff or student training, assemblies, drills relating to heat.
Evidence that the first in-season alert IS the instruction, i.e. no real pre-season phase.
How heat information reaches the school. Separates transmission failure from translation failure (rival explanation 1).
Circular, DoE portal, zonal WhatsApp, SMS, news/TV, IMD app, word of mouth.
Same day, previous evening, after school began, too late to act.
Alert or circular not received, or received by one actor only.
RQ2. How principals and teachers understand the information. Do NOT code 'divergence' here; find divergence later with a Matrix Coding Query on Role.
What Yellow, Orange or Red means to the respondent in terms of school action.
Tracking a worsening trajectory (Yellow to Orange to Red); who watches the forecast and how.
Understanding that conflicts with the source document or official clarification.
Respondent describes a common understanding across staff.
RQ2. Formal and perceived authority boundaries. Code only after checking what the formal rule says (fieldwork sequence step 4).
Actions the principal believes they may take without higher approval.
Waiting for DoE/DDE/zonal instruction before acting.
What a teacher may decide in the classroom without the principal.
Seeking permission or reporting upward; the route used.
Fear of blame, show-cause notices, audit, or parent complaints shaping the decision.
RQ3. Whether an authorised action can actually be carried out. Test this before attributing non-action to motivation or habit.
Supply failures, outages, broken coolers or fans.
Top-floor rooms, tin roofs, poor ventilation, no shade, exposed assembly area.
Too few staff to supervise, cover, or manage dispersal.
Constraints from exams, syllabus, PM POSHAN timing, assembly.
Double-shift constraints (morning girls / evening boys etc.).
Students walking, public transport, distance, peak-hour exposure on the way home.
RQ4. Whether the action protects children across school, travel and home, or transfers unmanaged risk.
Cancelling outdoor activity, moving to cooler rooms, water breaks.
Different handling for primary vs older pupils.
What happens when a child shows heat symptoms.
How early release is organised and communicated.
Children whose guardians cannot or will not collect them; holding arrangements; overnight stay question (Sakurai sensei feedback).
Action that shifts exposure or care burden outside the school (e.g. release at peak heat).
Whether experience changes future preparedness or policy.
Incident registers, attendance notes, heat logs.
Reporting problems or suggestions to zone/DoE/DDMA.
Changes made after a past season.
Same problem reported across seasons with no change.
Braun et al. (2011) contexts as described in talk. Fixed school facts (zone, shift, section) go in the School classification, not here.
Student age mix, enrolment, neighbourhood, history of the school.
Building, water, shade, power, budget.
Staff roles, experience, relationships, leadership style.
DoE/DDE/DDMA, parents, health services, local politics.
Realist-informed C-M-O. Code the reasoning or response that explains WHY an outcome happened. Link to context and outcome codes with relationships or memos.
Falling back on routines used for other situations (Sakurai et al., 2026).
Delay or inaction to avoid blame.
Actor sees early adjustment as legitimate and expected.
Effective local improvisation that could be institutionalised.
Practice that depends on one individual and would fail without them.
Formally compliant action that does not protect the child.
What the school actually did in the scenario or past event.
Acted before the severe alert.
Acted only after a live alert or explicit order.
Some indicated actions taken, others not.
No change in routine.
Heat compared with fire, earthquake or other hazards. Tests whether heat is less institutionalised rather than assuming it.
Fire drills, fire safety audits, NOC.
Earthquake drills, structural safety.
Floods, air pollution (GRAP), cold wave, COVID.
